INDUSTRY-PULP AND PAPER-EFFECT ON CANADIAN INDUSTRY OF LOANS TO FOREIGN COUNTRIES TO ESTABLISH PLANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appear tonight to elaborate on the reply given me by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) on the state of the pulp and paper industry in my district. This is an industry which is the lifeline of our economy in Newfoundland, one which the government should be protecting through every means available. This industry is hurting seriously, not only as a result of the loss of markets, markets which it is capable of competing for, but more so because of the narrow thinking of our government, which proclaims that
Adjournment Debate
what it is doing through the Export Development Corporation is helping the country.
Not only is the pulp and paper industry of Newfoundland seriously impeded by the destruction of its raw resource by the spruce budworm infestation, which if allowed to continue will destroy the viability of this industry in Newfoundland; not only is the industry hindered by the lack of a reasonable transportation policy, which is hurting the industry in cost effectiveness and competitiveness due to distance from markets; but the government, through the Export Development Corporation and CIDA, is assisting countries which are and have been potential customers by granting to them interest free loans, technical assistance and engineering expertise to establish industries which compete directly with us. The justification for this is that we are helping Canadian firms sell them equipment, thus creating jobs in Canada. This may be true to a point, Mr. Speaker, but it would be interesting to see in whose favour is this trade-off over the long term.
Notwithstanding that even part of the government's reasons are factual, what are we doing at the same time to allow our industry to compete after we have provided the financial assistance which, in the end, is directed to our foreign markets? A case in point is the related linerboard industry in Newfoundland which had to be closed down due to losses resulting from wood costs and lack of markets. What has the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce done other than to give the usual stock answer that it was not its responsibility, instead of the predecessor to the present minister taking the initiative and offering help?
If I can give the House an example, it was said that one of the reasons for the closure was inability to break through the market barrier. This linerboard mill in my province is perhaps the most modern in North America, yet it has to close down at a cost of some 2,000 jobs, affecting perhaps 4,100 jobs indirectly. Yet at the same time an American mill in Alabama, having increased its capacity just last summer, has announced expansion of its Union Camp Mill at a cost of $250 million so as to increase capacity by 1,000 tons a day.
It is time for the government to attempt to help our economy. It is fine to offer all kinds of incentives to establish new industries. I have no quarrel with such an objective. But what the government is doing really is ignoring what common sense dictates, namely, that we should be protecting, consolidating, and monitoring what we have, industries which have been successful through their own initiative and entrepreneurship but which are now hurting because of inflated costs of production. I refer particularly to the industries of Newfoundland which need assistance in view of their distance from markets. These industries in Newfoundland established themselves when conditions were normal, but now hesitate to continue operation because of encumbrances which exist as a result of the complacency of the responsible agencies of government.
I hope the parliamentary secretary will give me a more responsible answer than to relegate the matter to some other department. I hope he will give me something positive which I can take to those who require jobs, those who are losing jobs

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Veterans Affairs
subtopic: INDUSTRY-PULP AND PAPER-EFFECT ON CANADIAN INDUSTRY OF LOANS TO FOREIGN COUNTRIES TO ESTABLISH PLANTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Humber-St. George's-St. Barbe (Mr. Marshall). I must comment on the generous applause from all of my colleagues here in the House tonight. When I was just an ordinary backbencher, approximately 100 or 150 people would listen to me speak. I am sure Your Honour is aware of the size of my audience tonight. I had two briefings in order to come to the Chamber and give the hon. member an answer.
Perhaps there is a small misunderstanding of the nature and the reason for the operations of the Export Development Corporation. The corporation makes loans only to foreign buyers of Canadian-made equipment and Canadian services. The fact the equipment will be installed in a project in another country, which in theory or in fact may compete at a later date with a Canadian industry, would not be sufficient reason to deny jobs to those plants making equipment which the Export Development Corporation is financing. The only reason for such a course of action would be that it would prevent the development of a rival industry in another country.
The idea that Canada in this manner, or any other, could prevent another country developing a project is incorrect. Yet
somehow the idea persists in some quarters that if the Export Development Corporation did not finance the sale of Canadian equipment to these projects, then these projects would be halted. If one is aware how fierce international competition is in the sales of equipment to these projects, one would realize the projects will proceed easily without Canadian participation. The only measurable result of not financing such sales will be a drop of Canadian exports.
As the hon. Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Horner) pointed out, there is a paper industry in Poland. In making this loan we do not believe the Polish industry would serve any markets served by our country. Also we believe a loan made to them for the procurement of pulp and paper machinery in this country would create jobs needed in the manufacturing sector. This would ensure Canadians in our plants would have a chance to keep their jobs. Also they would make money to support their families, and indeed help the country.
Our industries should not be denied the chance to sell their products to other countries. This should be borne in mind by all members.
